title: Cost, latency and monitoring
notes: Cost is tokens times price, and every step re-sends the whole conversation, so each step costs more than the last.
Cut cost with shorter prompts, trimmed history, smaller models for simple steps, step limits and prompt caching; cut waiting with fewer steps and streaming.
Log tokens, cost, latency, tool errors and hand-offs for every request, and set alerts before a bill surprises you.

slides.title: Cost, latency and monitoring
slides.sub: What one answer costs, why loops get expensive, and how to watch it all
sentences: Every answer Scout gives costs money and takes time.
In this lesson you will price one real answer, see why long loops get expensive so fast, and learn to cut both cost and waiting time.
Then you will decide what to measure on every request, so a bill never surprises you again.

slides.title: How a model call is priced
slides.definition: What one model call costs: input tokens times the input price, plus output tokens times the output price.

analogy.label: Think of it as
analogy.text: A taxi that, at every new stop, charges you again for the whole route from home.

sentences: Start with how a model call is priced, in tokens, where a token is roughly three quarters of a word.
Input tokens are everything you send: the system prompt, the tool list and the whole conversation so far.
Output tokens are everything the model writes back, including its thinking and its tool calls.
Claude Opus 5.5 costs four dollars per million input tokens and twenty dollars per million output tokens.
Picture a taxi that, at every new stop, charges you again for the whole route from home.
That is exactly how an agent loop is billed, as the next two slides show.

slides.title: One answer, priced step by step

note.text: Cost = input × $4 + output × $20, per million tokens. About 5 cents an answer, or $20 a day at 400 tickets.

sentences: Let us price one real answer: Ana asks where her tent is, and Scout takes three steps.
Step one sends three thousand tokens and gets back a short call to get order: about one and a half cents.
Step two sends the whole conversation again, now with the order details, and calls track parcel.
Step three sends everything once more and writes the answer, which costs about two cents.
In total, ten and a half thousand input tokens and four hundred and fifty output tokens: about five cents.
At four hundred tickets a day, that is about twenty dollars a day, far less than the hours Leo's team gets back.

slides.title: Why a loop gets expensive fast
slides.scenario: A tool keeps failing and Scout keeps retrying. Each attempt adds about 500 tokens to the conversation.

steps.text: Sends 3,000 tokens. Input costs about 1 cent.
Sends 7,500 tokens. About 3 cents for this step alone.
Sends 52,500 tokens. About 21 cents for one step.
Sends about 500,000 tokens. About $2 for one step.

result.text: Each step costs more than the last, so the total grows far faster than the step count.

sentences: Now the dangerous part: the model remembers nothing between calls, so every step re-sends the whole conversation.
Imagine a tool that keeps failing, where each failed attempt adds about five hundred tokens to the history.
By step ten, a single step sends seven and a half thousand tokens, about three cents.
By step one hundred, one step on its own costs about twenty one cents.
By step one thousand, one step sends half a million tokens and costs about two dollars.
Every step costs more than the one before, so the total grows much faster than the number of steps.
That is how a weekend loop on a broken tool turned into an eighteen hundred dollar bill.

slides.title: Five ways to cut the cost

spokes.label: Shorter prompts
spokes.sub: cut what the model never uses

spokes.label: Step limits
spokes.sub: a hard stop on every loop

note.text: Change one thing at a time, then re-run your Module 5 tests to check quality held.

sentences: So how do you bring the cost per answer down?
First, shorter prompts: cut instructions and examples the model never actually uses.
Second, trim the history: keep the recent turns and the key facts, as you did in Module 4.
Third, use a smaller model for simple steps; Claude Haiku 5.5 costs forty times less than Opus 5.5 and is fine for sorting a ticket.
Fourth, put a step limit on every loop, so one request can never run away.
Fifth, prompt caching lets the provider reuse the unchanged start of your prompt, such as the system prompt and tool list, at a much lower price.
Change one thing at a time, and re-run your Module 5 tests to make sure quality held.

slides.title: Where the waiting time goes

note.text: Latency adds up across steps. Fewer steps, smaller models and streaming make Scout feel fast.

sentences: Latency is the time the customer waits, and in an agent it adds up across the steps.
Each model call takes a few seconds, because the model reads everything, thinks, and writes its answer token by token.
Each tool call adds its own time, and a slow carrier API can add many more seconds.
Two model calls and one tool already make an eight second wait, and three or four calls make it longer.
Streaming helps: the reply appears word by word as it is written, so the customer sees progress instead of a blank screen.
Fewer steps, smaller models for quick steps, and streaming are your three main tools against waiting.

slides.title: Streaming a reply with the SDK
slides.lead: Swap messages.create for messages.stream, and send each piece of text as soon as it arrives.

rows.out: each new piece of text, as it is written
words appear on the customer's screen
the full message, with usage for the log

aside.label: In an agent
aside.text: Stream every model call and pass only the text to the customer. Tool calls happen quietly in between.

sentences: Here is what streaming looks like with the SDK.
Instead of messages create, you call messages stream, with exactly the same arguments.
Then you loop over the text stream, which hands you each new piece of text as soon as it is written.
Each piece goes straight to the customer's screen, so they watch the answer appear.
At the end you still get the full message, with the usage numbers your cost log needs.
In an agent, stream every call and pass only the text on; the tool calls happen quietly in between.

slides.title: What to watch, and when to shout
sentences: Finally, monitoring, because you cannot fix what you cannot see.
For every request, log one line with the tokens, the cost, the latency, the tools used, any tool errors and whether Scout handed off.
Your Module 5 trace shows one conversation in detail; these log lines show the whole day at a glance.
From the logs, watch the trends: spend per day, the slowest replies, and how often Scout hands off or hits errors.
A sudden jump in hand-offs or tool errors usually means a tool or an API key has broken.
Then set alerts that message a person, for example when spend passes fifty dollars in a day or tool errors pass ten percent.
Also set a monthly spend limit in your provider account, as a last safety net.
Alerts like these would have caught the eighteen hundred dollar weekend within hours, not on Monday.

slides.title: Recap: cost, latency and monitoring

points.text: Cost is tokens times price: Opus 5.5 is $4 in, $20 out per million.
Each step re-sends the conversation, so long loops get expensive fast.
Cut cost: shorter prompts, trimmed history, smaller models, limits, caching.
Latency adds up across steps; stream the reply so it feels fast.
Log every request and alert on spend, errors and slow replies.

sentences: Here is what to take away.
Cost is tokens times price, and for Opus 5.5 that is four dollars per million in and twenty per million out.
Every step re-sends the whole conversation, so a long loop gets expensive very fast.
Shorter prompts, trimmed history, smaller models for simple steps, step limits and caching all cut the bill.
Latency adds up across steps, and streaming the reply makes the wait feel short.
And log every request, then set alerts on spend, errors and slow replies.
Next, you will put Scout on a server where customers can reach it.

midQuiz.q: A step sends 4,000 input tokens and gets 250 output tokens on Opus 5.5 ($4 in, $20 out per million). What does it cost?
midQuiz.hint: Work out the input cost and the output cost separately, then add them.

midQuiz.q: Why does step 100 of a looping agent cost far more than step 1?
options: The provider charges more after many calls in a row
Every step re-sends the whole conversation, which keeps growing
Output tokens get more expensive as a chat goes on
midQuiz.explain: The model remembers nothing between calls, so each step sends the full history again. More history means more input tokens on every single step.
midQuiz.hint: What does each step have to send to the model?

endQuiz.q: Scout's replies take 12 seconds at lunchtime. Which change helps most without hurting the answers?
options: Stream the reply and use a smaller model for simple steps
Raise max_tokens so the model has more room to answer
Add a second model call that double-checks every reply
endQuiz.explain: Streaming shows words straight away, and a small model is quicker for simple steps such as sorting the question. More room or an extra check only adds time.
endQuiz.hint: Which option removes waiting, rather than adding more work?

endQuiz.q: Overnight, Scout's hand-offs jump from 5% to 40% of requests. What is the most likely cause?
options: Customers suddenly started asking much harder questions
A tool or an API key has broken, so Scout keeps handing off
The model provider changed its prices overnight
endQuiz.explain: A sudden jump overnight points to something that broke, not a slow change in customers. Check the tool errors in the logs first.
endQuiz.hint: Slow changes usually come from customers; sudden ones usually come from something breaking.
